entries.clue: Message hidden in alliterative passage? (4)

indicatorNotes.passage: A passage is a stretch of text, and the answer is a stretch running through the clue's own words.

blocks.note: the letters straddle three words: the last of the first, all of the second, the first of the third

annotation.surface: A literary critic spotting a secret message buried in a line of verse that plays on repeated sounds.
annotation.walkthrough: "Hidden" looks like the indicator, but it is fodder: its last letter starts the answer. A nina is a hidden message in a crossword grid, named after the daughter Al Hirschfeld hid in his drawings, and this grid carries one.
annotation.definitionFit: Solvers use nina for a message concealed in a crossword grid, a borrowing from the name Al Hirschfeld hid in his cartoons.

entries.clue: Those who spread filth include source of plot revelations (8)

indicatorNotes.include: To include something is to take it inside, so the first word goes around the next.
indicatorNotes.source of: The source of a river is where it starts, so the source of a word is its opening letter.

blocks.note: people who soil things spread dirt around
the opening letter of 'plot'

annotation.surface: Gossip-mongers dishing the dirt, with some story-leaking thrown into the mix.
annotation.walkthrough: The word "plot" does two jobs: its first letter goes inside, and it also sits in the definition. SOILERS is a rare word, but it means just what it looks like.
annotation.definitionFit: Spoilers are details that give away how a film, book or show turns out, spoiling the surprise for anyone who has not seen it.

entries.clue: Consequence of lob? (6)

blocks.note: the result or outcome of something, how it finally turns out
split into two words, the answer describes a lob: a ball hit high into the air

annotation.surface: A tennis player wondering what will come of a high, looping return.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the second definition as playful: UPSHOT split into two words describes a lob. "Of" joins the two meanings.
annotation.definitionFit: The upshot is the final result or outcome, and a lob, read as two words, is an up shot.

entries.clue: How one is knocked as team trails? (8)

blocks.note: a team is a side, as in a football side
trails are paths, or ways

annotation.surface: A supporter left reeling as their team falls behind.
annotation.walkthrough: "Trails" pretends to be a verb for losing a match; it is really a noun for paths. "Knocked sideways" means badly shaken.
annotation.definitionFit: To be knocked sideways is to be badly shaken or stunned, so SIDEWAYS completes the idiom for how a shock knocks you.

entries.clue: Coward’s spirit thusly seen in barrel drunk by that man? (6)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition asks for the word Noël Coward put before 'Spirit' in his play's title, an adjective standing in the phrase rather than a synonym for it.

blocks.note: B is a standard abbreviation for barrel
lit is slang for drunk
the pronoun for 'that man'

annotation.surface: A cowardly man topping up his nerve with spirits from a barrel.
annotation.walkthrough: "Coward" has its capital for a reason: it is Noël Coward, whose comedy is Blithe Spirit. The capital hides at the start of the sentence, so the cowardly drinker is the false picture.
annotation.definitionFit: Blithe Spirit is Noël Coward's comedy about a ghostly first wife, so BLITHE is how Coward described his spirit; it also means cheerfully carefree.

entries.clue: Strike a blow to groin having struck backside previously? (4)

indicatorNotes.backside: The backside of anything is its rear end, so the backside of a word is its final letter.

blocks.note: the final letter of 'struck'
née marks a woman's previous surname, as in Smith née Jones

annotation.surface: A fight in which someone kicked in the rear hits back lower down.
annotation.walkthrough: "Backside" looks like part of the brawl but only picks out the last letter of "struck". Née comes from French and means 'born', so it marks what someone was previously called.
annotation.definitionFit: To knee someone is to hit them with your knee, and the groin is the classic target of that blow.

entries.clue: 20ac to nip out in car (7)

indicatorNotes.in: One thing being in another means it sits inside it, so the first piece goes inside the second.

blocks.note: a limo is a limousine, a large car
to pop out somewhere is to nip out briefly

annotation.surface: Someone slipping out for a quick errand in the car.
annotation.walkthrough: The cross-reference points to the answer at 20 across, RIVER, so the definition just says 'a river'. The Limpopo is Kipling's river in the Just So Story about the Elephant's Child, the theme of this puzzle.
annotation.definitionFit: The Limpopo is a river in southern Africa, Kipling's 'great grey-green, greasy Limpopo River' in the Just So Stories.

entries.clue: Author’s copyright, say, written in artificial language lacking in use (7)

indicatorNotes.written in: Something written in a text is put inside it, so these letters go inside the others.
indicatorNotes.lacking: Lacking something means going without it, so those letters are taken away.

blocks.note: Klingon is the language invented for the Star Trek aliens
a machine in use is on; these letters are removed
copyright is one kind of IP, intellectual property

annotation.surface: A writer's rights being set out in some made-up language that nobody uses.
annotation.walkthrough: "Say" signals an example: copyright is one form of intellectual property. The "’s" stands for 'is', joining the author to the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Rudyard Kipling was the author of the Just So Stories, which include the Elephant's Child tale behind this puzzle's theme.

entries.clue: Cloth sample in Mombasa rickshaw (4)

indicatorNotes.sample in: A sample is a small piece taken from something larger, so the answer is a piece taken from the words that follow.

blocks.note: the letters straddle the two words: the last two of the port's name and the first two of the vehicle

annotation.surface: A textile trader carrying fabric samples through Mombasa by rickshaw.
annotation.walkthrough: "Sample" reads like a fabric swatch, which fits "cloth", but it is doing the hiding. Mombasa is a port in Kenya.
annotation.definitionFit: A sari is a long length of cloth draped around the body, the traditional dress of women in South Asia, so the garment is itself a cloth.

entries.clue: Digital discomfort caused as actor pressed remote (9)

indicatorNotes.pressed: Something pressed is squashed out of its old shape, so these letters are rearranged.

blocks.note: a ham is an actor who overacts
the six letters of 'remote' rearranged

annotation.surface: A sore thumb from jabbing at a TV remote control.
annotation.walkthrough: "Digital" suggests electronics and a finger on a button; the digit here is a toe. A ham is a crossword's usual actor.
annotation.definitionFit: Toes are digits, and hammertoe, a toe bent permanently at the middle joint, is a painful condition of one.

entries.clue: Worn-out, he meant to work out (4-5)

indicatorNotes.work out: To work something out is to solve it by rearranging it, so these letters are sorted into a new order.

blocks.note: the nine letters of 'he meant to' rearranged

annotation.surface: Someone exhausted, though he had meant to get to the gym.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface echoes itself: "Worn-out" and "work out" look like the start and end of the same idea. Only the second is an instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Moth-eaten clothes are full of holes where moths fed on them, and the word also means shabby and worn-out in general.

entries.clue: Worry after starts to get ready in August (5)

indicatorNotes.after: In an across entry, something coming after another thing is placed behind it, so the first word follows the letters that come next.
indicatorNotes.starts to: The starts of words are their first letters, so only those letters are kept.

blocks.note: the first letters of 'get' and 'ready'
something that eats at you worries you, as in 'what's eating you?'

annotation.surface: Someone fretting about preparations for a summer holiday.
annotation.walkthrough: "August" has a capital only because it follows "in" in the surface; the definition is the adjective meaning grand, not the month.
annotation.definitionFit: August as an adjective means grand and distinguished, a plain synonym for great in the sense of eminent.

entries.clue: Driver’s aim is to be ecologically responsible (5)

blocks.note: a golfer's drive is aimed at the closely mown area round the hole
the colour that stands for environmental politics

annotation.surface: A motorist resolving to drive in an environmentally friendly way.
annotation.walkthrough: The driver is a golf club, or the golfer swinging it, not a motorist. The surface brings in electric cars to make the environmental sense look like the only one.
annotation.definitionFit: The green is the target of a golfer's approach, and green also means environmentally responsible.

entries.clue: Rated clue quid pro quo? (5-3)

blocks.note: the plain sense: something given in exchange for something else
the answer read as a clue: TRADE, then OFF telling you to rearrange it, produces the word 'rated'

annotation.surface: Someone giving a clue a score, as if marking one in exchange for another.
annotation.walkthrough: This is a reverse clue: the answer works as wordplay, and "Rated" is what it produces. TRADE with "off" as an anagram indicator gives RATED.
annotation.definitionFit: A trade-off is an exchange where you give up one thing to get another, which is exactly what quid pro quo means in Latin: 'something for something'.

entries.clue: Passion for first under any circumstances (5)

indicatorNotes.first: The first of a word is its opening letter, so only that letter is used.

blocks.note: the opening letter of 'for'
ever means at any time or in any case, as in 'if ever'

annotation.surface: A declaration that one's love must always come first, whatever happens.
annotation.walkthrough: "For first" reads as 'putting it first'; it gives the first letter of "for". The fever trees of the Limpopo complete the theme with 16 across.
annotation.definitionFit: A fever is a state of intense excitement or passion, as in 'a fever of anticipation'.

entries.clue: Softies on the right left (4)

blocks.note: a wet is a feeble, soft person
Margaret Thatcher called the more left-leaning Conservative MPs, those on the right who leant left, by a word meaning drippy

annotation.surface: Politicians on the right being written off as spineless for drifting leftward.
annotation.walkthrough: "Right left" looks like two directions cancelling out, but it describes one group: moderate Tories of the 1980s whom Thatcher's allies dismissed as wets.
annotation.definitionFit: A wet is a feeble, ineffectual person, and in British politics the Wets were the more moderate, left-leaning members of Thatcher's Conservative party.

entries.clue: 20ac found in 20ac in woods (5)

indicatorNotes.found in: Something found in a place is inside it, so the first piece goes inside the second.

blocks.note: the Tees is a river in north-east England
R is the standard abbreviation for river

annotation.surface: A river running through another river in a wood, a riddle of cross-references.
annotation.walkthrough: Both cross-references point to RIVER at 20 across, but each works differently: one gives the abbreviation R, the other a real river. The Limpopo's fever trees are part of the theme.
annotation.definitionFit: Woods are a mass of trees, and the plural answer is a plain synonym for woods when the timber is standing.

entries.clue: Thrashed out addition to the capital’s skyline (3,5)

indicatorNotes.out: Letters that are out are out of their places, so they must be put back in a new order.

blocks.note: the eight letters of 'thrashed' rearranged

annotation.surface: Planners arguing over a new tower for London until the matter is settled.
annotation.walkthrough: "Thrashed out" reads as a phrase meaning 'debated to a conclusion', which suits a planning row; split, it is fodder plus instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: The Shard is the glass skyscraper finished in 2012 beside London Bridge station, a recent and prominent addition to London's skyline.

entries.clue: 20ac retired fading star (4)

indicatorNotes.retired: To retire is to go back or withdraw, so the word is read backwards.

blocks.note: the Avon is a river, and several English rivers carry the name

annotation.surface: A star who has quit the stage and whose fame is dimming.
annotation.walkthrough: The "fading star" looks like a has-been celebrity; it is an astronomical nova, which blazes up and then dims back down.
annotation.definitionFit: A nova is a star that suddenly flares much brighter and then fades over weeks or months back towards its old brightness.

entries.clue: Direct a neat dodge to collect interest on the street (8)

indicatorNotes.dodge: To dodge is to swerve and shift about, so these letters move into a new order.
indicatorNotes.to collect: To collect something is to take it in, so the rearranged letters go around the next piece.

blocks.note: the letters of 'a neat' rearranged
vig, short for vigorish, is street slang for the interest a loan shark charges

annotation.surface: A loan shark's crafty scheme for collecting interest on the street.
annotation.walkthrough: "On the street" flags slang: the vig is an American gambling and loan-shark word for the cut or interest taken. "Dodge" works as a noun in the surface and as an instruction in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: To navigate is to steer or direct a course, and to direct someone is to show them the way, so the two verbs share the guiding sense.

entries.clue: Cosiest room in pub with guest not fit for all (8)

indicatorNotes.not: Not means without, so the letter that follows is taken out.

blocks.note: the snug is a small, cosy side room in a British pub
the word as written
U is the British film rating for universal, fit for all ages; this letter is removed

annotation.surface: A pub's cosiest room, with a guest who turns out to be unsuitable company.
annotation.walkthrough: "Not fit for all" looks like it describes the guest; really it drops U, the film certificate for films anyone can see.
annotation.definitionFit: Snug means warm and cosy, so its superlative, snuggest, is a plain synonym for cosiest.

entries.clue: Like café might be when smothered by 22 (6)

indicatorNotes.smothered by: Something smothered by another thing is wrapped up inside it, so the first piece goes inside the second.

blocks.note: the answer to 22 across
as and when both mean 'at the time that'

annotation.surface: A café smothered in something grey and unappetising.
annotation.walkthrough: A greasy spoon is British slang for a cheap café serving fried food. Greasy is also one of the Limpopo's adjectives in Kipling's line.
annotation.definitionFit: A greasy spoon is a cheap café serving fried food, so greasy is what a café might be called.

entries.clue: Banker’s club lost its head (5)

indicatorNotes.lost its head: A word that has lost its head has lost its first letter.

blocks.note: a driver is the golf club used for long tee shots

annotation.surface: A banker's gentlemen's club in disarray after its chairman is ousted.
annotation.walkthrough: "Banker" is a crossword staple for a river, which has banks. The "’s" stands for 'is'.
annotation.definitionFit: A river has banks, so a banker in crossword terms is something with banks; it is a playful coinage rather than a dictionary sense.

entries.clue: Sappers’ prompt relief (6)

blocks.note: the sappers are the RE, the Royal Engineers, and the possessive adds S
an actor's cue is the prompt to speak

annotation.surface: Army engineers arriving promptly to bring relief to a besieged town.
annotation.walkthrough: "Prompt" pretends to be an adjective meaning quick; it is the noun, a cue. The elephant's child was rescued from the crocodile in Kipling's story.
annotation.definitionFit: Relief in the military sense is the rescue of a besieged place, as in the relief of Mafeking.

entries.clue: Those making trunk calls when footballer rejected by county (9)

indicatorNotes.rejected: Something rejected is thrown back, so the name is read backwards.

blocks.note: Pelé, the Brazilian footballer, reversed
Hants is the short form of Hampshire, an English county

annotation.surface: A footballer left out of a county side, the phone lines buzzing with long-distance calls.
annotation.walkthrough: "Trunk calls" is old British for long-distance phone calls; here the trunks are elephants' and the calls are trumpeting. The elephant's child got its trunk in Kipling's story.
annotation.definitionFit: Elephants trumpet through their trunks, so their calls are trunk calls, punning on the old British term for long-distance phone calls.

entries.clue: Before final curtain, First Lady will be flush (4)

indicatorNotes.Before: In a down entry, what comes before sits above, so the first piece goes on top of the second.
indicatorNotes.final: The final part of a word is its last letter.

blocks.note: in Genesis Eve is the first woman
the last letter of 'curtain'

annotation.surface: A president's wife taking her last bow and coming out in the money.
annotation.walkthrough: "First Lady" suggests the White House; it is Eve, the first woman. "Flush" can mean rich, but here it means level with something.
annotation.definitionFit: Flush means level, with no part sticking out, as in a door flush with the wall, which is what even means too.

entries.clue: Drab moving from black to white when on scale? (4)

annotation.definition2: moving from black to white when on scale

blocks.note: dull and colourless

blocks.clueFragment: moving from black to white when on scale?
blocks.note: the tones a scale of shades passes through between black and white, the colour the scale is named after

annotation.surface: A dull object sliding along a scale from dark to light.
annotation.walkthrough: The "scale" is a greyscale, the tonal range used for black-and-white images. The question mark marks the second definition as descriptive rather than a dictionary one.
annotation.definitionFit: Grey means dull and lifeless, and every tone between black and white on a greyscale is a shade of grey.

entries.clue: Take home note, following musical talent (4)

indicatorNotes.following: In a down entry, something following another thing comes after it, so the note goes below the talent.

blocks.note: a good ear is a talent for hearing music
N is the standard abbreviation for note

annotation.surface: A musician taking home a banknote on the strength of their talent.
annotation.walkthrough: "Take home" is the pay sense, as in take-home pay. N for note is the dictionary abbreviation, not a musical note.
annotation.definitionFit: Take-home pay is what you earn after deductions, so to take home a sum is to earn it.

entries.clue: Frantic when fool includes sex education (7)

indicatorNotes.includes: To include something is to take it inside, so the fool goes around the next letters.

blocks.note: berk is British slang for a fool
RSE, Relationships and Sex Education, is the school subject in England

annotation.surface: A fool teaching sex education and sending the class into a panic.
annotation.walkthrough: The obvious SE for "sex education" leaves you one R short; the English school subject is called RSE.
annotation.definitionFit: Berserk means wild and out of control, from the Norse berserkers who fought in a frenzy, so it is a plain synonym for frantic.

entries.clue: French street to get quiet routine back during break (7)

indicatorNotes.back: Going back is going in reverse, so the word is read backwards.
indicatorNotes.during: What happens during something happens inside its span, so these letters go inside the street.

blocks.note: rue is French for street
p, piano, is the musical instruction to play quietly
a rut is a dull routine, reversed

annotation.surface: A Parisian street finding its peace and routine again during a holiday.
annotation.walkthrough: "Break" looks like a holiday that interrupts the routine; it is the definition. P for quiet comes from musical notation.
annotation.definitionFit: A rupture is a break or tear, as in a burst pipe, so the noun is a plain synonym for break.
